title: Linux Essentials
subtitle: 20 questions across files, permissions, packages, processes, networking and security

questions.q: Which command copies a directory and ALL of its contents recursively?
questions.note: The -r (or --recursive) flag tells cp to descend into subdirectories. Without it, cp refuses to copy a directory.

explain.correct: cp -r recurses into the directory tree, copying every file and subdirectory to the destination.
wrong: cp without -r fails with 'omitting directory' — it cannot copy directories without the recursive flag.
mv moves (renames) the directory rather than copying it; the original is removed.
cp -p preserves timestamps and permissions but does NOT recurse into directories on its own.

questions.q: You run: ln file.txt hardlink.txt — then delete file.txt. What happens to hardlink.txt?
options: It becomes a broken symbolic link
It still contains the full file data
questions.note: Hard links share the same inode. The data is only removed when the last hard link (the last directory entry pointing to that inode) is deleted.

explain.correct: Both names point to the same inode. Deleting one name decrements the link count but the data survives until the count reaches zero.
wrong: Broken symbolic links occur when the target of a symlink is deleted. A hard link is not a symlink — it is a second directory entry for the same inode, so it cannot become 'broken'.
Only the name file.txt is removed from the directory. The inode and its data remain as long as hardlink.txt exists.
/dev/null is a special device file. Hard links have no concept of a null fallback destination.

questions.q: Which find command locates all regular files larger than 10 MB under /var?
questions.note: find -size +10M means 'greater than 10 mebibytes'. The + prefix means strictly more than, and M is the mebibyte unit suffix.

explain.correct: -type f restricts results to regular files and -size +10M matches files strictly larger than 10 MB.
wrong: This restricts the search to files whose name ends in .log AND matches exactly 10 MB — not larger than 10 MB, and not all file types.
locate searches a pre-built filename database. It has no -size option for filtering by file size.
-type d matches directories, not regular files. This would find directories larger than 10 MB, not files.

questions.q: What does the grep -v flag do?
options: Prints lines that do NOT match the pattern
Counts the number of matching lines
questions.note: grep -v inverts the match, printing every line that does not contain the pattern — useful for filtering out noise from command output.

explain.correct: -v stands for 'invert match', so grep outputs all lines where the pattern is absent.
wrong: Printing only matching lines is the default grep behavior with no special flags — no -v needed.
grep -c counts matching lines and prints only the total count, not the lines themselves.
grep -r (or --recursive) searches through directories. -v has nothing to do with recursion.

questions.q: Which sed command replaces every occurrence of 'cat' with 'dog' IN-PLACE in file.txt?
questions.note: sed -i edits the file in place. The /g flag on the substitution replaces all occurrences per line, not just the first match.

explain.correct: -i tells sed to write changes back to the original file. The /g flag replaces all matches on each line, not only the first.
wrong: Without -i, sed writes to stdout only — the file is unchanged. Without /g, only the first occurrence per line is replaced.
Redirecting sed's output to the SAME file with > truncates the file to zero bytes before sed can read it, resulting in an empty file.
awk can substitute with gsub(), but this snippet is missing a print statement so it produces no output, and it does not modify the file in place.

questions.q: In the pipeline: cat /etc/passwd | awk -F: '{print $1}', what does -F: set?
options: The field (column) separator used when splitting each input line
A filter that keeps only lines containing a colon
questions.note: awk's -F option sets the input field separator. With -F: each line is split on colons, so $1 is the username column in /etc/passwd.

explain.correct: -F: tells awk to split each input line on the colon character, making $1 the first field (the username in /etc/passwd).
wrong: The output field separator in awk is OFS, set with -v OFS=':' or inside the BEGIN block — not -F.
Line selection in awk uses the NR variable (e.g., NR==3). -F does not target a line number.
-F sets the input field delimiter for splitting; it does not act as a grep-style filter to match or reject lines.

questions.q: What file descriptor number represents stderr?
questions.note: Linux assigns fd 0 to stdin, fd 1 to stdout, and fd 2 to stderr. Redirect stderr with 2> or combine it with stdout using 2>&1.

explain.correct: File descriptor 2 is stderr. Redirecting it with 2>/dev/null suppresses error messages from a command.
wrong: File descriptor 0 is stdin — the standard input stream, where keyboard input arrives by default.
File descriptor 1 is stdout — the standard output stream where normal command output is written.
File descriptor 3 and above are available for user-opened files; they are not pre-assigned system streams.

questions.q: Which command adds existing user 'alice' to supplementary group 'docker' WITHOUT removing her from other groups?
questions.note: usermod -aG appends the user to the group. Omitting -a with -G replaces ALL supplementary groups, which can break existing access.

explain.correct: -a (append) combined with -G adds docker to alice's supplementary groups while preserving all existing group memberships.
wrong: usermod -g (lowercase) changes the user's PRIMARY group, not supplementary groups, and does not append to anything.
groupadd creates a new group; it does not accept a username to add members and will error if the group already exists.
useradd is for creating new users. Running it on an existing username produces an error; it does not modify existing accounts.

questions.q: A file has permissions 755. What can members of the file's GROUP do?
questions.note: Octal 755 breaks down as: owner=7 (rwx), group=5 (r-x), others=5 (r-x). The group digit 5 = read(4) + execute(1).

explain.correct: The middle octal digit 5 = 4(read) + 1(execute). Group members can read and execute the file but cannot write to it.
wrong: Read+write+execute (digit 7) applies to the owner only in 755, not to the group or others.
Read-only would be digit 4 in the group position. The digit 5 adds execute permission on top of read.
No access would be digit 0 in the group position. Digit 5 grants both read and execute.

questions.q: Which special permission bit on /tmp prevents users from deleting each other's files?
questions.note: The sticky bit on a world-writable directory means only the file owner or root can delete or rename files within it, even if others have write permission on the directory.

explain.correct: The sticky bit (octal 1000, shown as 't' in ls -l) on /tmp restricts deletion so each user can only remove their own files.
wrong: SUID (4xxx) on an executable runs the program as the file's owner (e.g., passwd runs as root). It has no effect on directory deletion restrictions.
SGID (2xxx) on a directory causes new files to inherit the directory's group. It does not prevent users from deleting each other's files.
umask is a creation mask that reduces permissions on newly created files and directories. It is not a special permission bit applied to existing directories.

questions.q: On a Debian/Ubuntu system, which command installs a package AND resolves dependencies automatically?
questions.note: apt is the high-level front-end for Debian package management. It contacts repositories and automatically downloads and installs all required dependencies.

explain.correct: apt install contacts configured repositories, resolves the full dependency tree, and installs the package and all its dependencies.
wrong: dpkg is the low-level Debian package tool. It installs a local .deb file but does NOT resolve or download missing dependencies automatically.
rpm is the low-level Red Hat package tool used on RHEL/Fedora systems — not Debian/Ubuntu — and it also does not resolve dependencies.
zypper is the package manager for openSUSE/SUSE Linux Enterprise. It is not available on Debian/Ubuntu systems.

questions.q: On RHEL 8/9, which command has REPLACED yum as the primary package manager?
questions.note: DNF (Dandified YUM) replaced yum as the default in Fedora 22 and RHEL 8. It delivers better dependency resolution and a cleaner plugin API.

explain.correct: dnf is the modern package manager for RHEL 8/9 and Fedora. On RHEL 8+, the yum command is itself a symbolic link to dnf.
wrong: apt is the high-level package manager for Debian/Ubuntu systems. It is not available on RHEL by default.
zypper is the package manager for openSUSE and SUSE Linux Enterprise — not RHEL.
pacman is the package manager for Arch Linux and its derivatives. It is not used on RHEL.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'systemctl start nginx' and 'systemctl enable nginx'?
options: start makes it persist at boot; enable starts it now
start runs it now; enable makes it start automatically at boot
They are identical — both start and persist the service
enable installs the package; start launches it
questions.note: start and enable are independent. Use 'systemctl enable --now nginx' to both enable at boot AND start it immediately in one command.

explain.correct: systemctl start launches the service in the current session only. systemctl enable creates a symlink in the appropriate wants directory so the service starts at boot.
wrong: This reverses the meaning of the two commands. start affects only the current running session; enable affects boot-time behavior.
They are not identical. start has no effect on boot configuration, and enable does not start the service immediately.
Package installation is handled by apt/dnf/zypper — not systemctl. enable only controls the boot-time activation symlink.

questions.q: Which journalctl flag shows log entries from the CURRENT boot only?
questions.note: journalctl -b filters to the current boot. Use -b -1 for the previous boot, -b -2 for two boots ago, and so on.

explain.correct: -b filters the journal to entries from the current boot session, making it easier to see what happened since the last reboot.
wrong: journalctl -f follows the journal in real time (like tail -f), showing new entries as they arrive. It does not filter by boot.
journalctl -u <unit> filters entries for a specific systemd service unit. It does not filter by boot session.
journalctl -r shows entries in reverse chronological order (newest first) across all boots. It does not filter to the current boot.

questions.q: A cron entry reads: 30 2 * * 1 /usr/bin/backup.sh — when does it run?
options: On the 1st of every month at 2:30 AM
questions.note: Cron fields (left to right): minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Day-of-week 1 = Monday. Asterisks in fields 3 and 4 mean every day and every month.

explain.correct: minute=30, hour=2, dom=*, month=*, dow=1 (Monday). The script runs at exactly 2:30 AM every Monday.
wrong: Every day at 2:30 AM would require '30 2 * * *' with an asterisk in the day-of-week field. The '1' in position 5 restricts it to Mondays.
'Every 30 minutes' would require '*/30' in the minute field (position 1). The value '30' means 'at minute 30' — a fixed time, not an interval.
The 1st of each month would require a '1' in the day-of-MONTH field (position 3). Here the '1' is in the day-of-WEEK field (position 5).

questions.q: Which tool schedules a one-time command to run at a specific future time?
questions.note: The 'at' command accepts a time specification (e.g., 'at 3pm tomorrow') and runs the queued commands once. Use 'atq' to list pending jobs.

explain.correct: at schedules a one-time task. After running 'at <time>', you type the command(s) and press Ctrl+D to submit the job for single execution.
wrong: cron is designed for RECURRING scheduled jobs. Each crontab entry runs repeatedly on its schedule — it is not intended for single one-time execution.
anacron is designed for recurring periodic jobs that may have been missed (e.g., on laptops that are off at night). It does not schedule one-time future commands.
systemd-run --timer can schedule transient units but is not the standard beginner-level tool for one-time scheduling. 'at' is the conventional answer in this course.

questions.q: Which partition table format supports more than 4 primary partitions and disks larger than 2 TB?
questions.note: GPT (GUID Partition Table) supports up to 128 partitions by default and uses 64-bit LBA addressing, supporting disks far beyond 2 TB.

explain.correct: GPT removes MBR's hard limit of 4 primary partitions and the ~2 TB disk size ceiling. Use gdisk or parted to create GPT partition tables.
wrong: MBR is limited to 4 primary partitions (or 3 primary + 1 extended) and a maximum addressable disk size of ~2 TB using 512-byte sectors.
ext4 is a filesystem type — it formats the space inside a partition. Partition tables and filesystems are separate layers of disk organization.
LVM (Logical Volume Manager) is a volume management layer that sits on top of partitions. It is not a partition table format.

questions.q: Which filesystem is the default on RHEL 9 and CANNOT be shrunk?
questions.note: XFS is the default filesystem for RHEL 7 and later. It supports online growing but shrinking is not supported at all — you must back up, reformat, and restore.

explain.correct: XFS is RHEL's default filesystem. It can be grown while mounted but cannot be shrunk — not online, not offline.
wrong: ext4 is the traditional Linux filesystem and the default on Debian/Ubuntu. It CAN be shrunk offline with resize2fs. It is not the RHEL 9 default.
btrfs supports both online grow and shrink operations, and adds built-in snapshotting. It is not the RHEL 9 default.
vfat is used for FAT32 partitions such as EFI system partitions. It is not a general-purpose Linux root filesystem.

questions.q: You run 'ip addr add 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0'. After reboot, the address is gone. Why?
options: ip addr requires root to persist changes
ip addr changes are runtime-only; use nmcli or connection files to persist
The kernel rejected the address as a duplicate
/etc/hosts must be updated to make IP addresses permanent
questions.note: The ip command modifies only the kernel's live network state. On reboot, the kernel reinitializes from persistent configuration, discarding runtime changes.

explain.correct: ip addr modifies only the running kernel state. To survive reboots, use 'nmcli connection modify' or edit the appropriate network configuration file for your distribution.
wrong: Root (sudo) is typically required to run ip addr add, but elevated privilege does not make the change persistent. It still only modifies runtime state.
The kernel accepts the ip addr command immediately — the address is active until reboot. The issue is persistence, not rejection.
/etc/hosts maps hostnames to IP addresses for name resolution. It has no role in configuring or persisting network interface addresses.

questions.q: Which SSH private key permission is required for SSH to accept and use the key?
questions.note: SSH enforces strict permissions on private keys. If the key is readable by group or others, SSH refuses it with 'Permissions are too open' and exits.

explain.correct: 600 (rw-------) means only the owner can read and write the key. SSH requires this — no group or other access is permitted on private keys.
wrong: 644 allows group and others to read the private key. SSH will refuse to use it and print an error that the permissions are too open.
755 grants execute permission and allows group and others to read the file. SSH will reject any private key readable by group or others.
777 grants full read/write/execute to everyone. SSH absolutely refuses private keys with world-readable or world-writable permissions.
